title: Rebranding After an Acquisition: Updating Your Visual Identity
description: Plan a visual identity update after an acquisition: logo, typography, color, website, and rollout, with a real Airport Executive logo redesign example.
body:
After an acquisition, the business may have a new direction while its visual identity still reflects the past.

The logo, typography, colors, website, and everyday materials need to express that direction consistently.

The goal is to make the business look like one coherent brand while preserving useful recognition.

This guide focuses on the visual identity: what to retain, what to redesign, and how to roll it out across digital and physical applications.

If the company name is changing too, resolve that decision before finalizing the identity.

Define what the visual identity needs to communicate

Write a short description of what customers will experience differently under the new ownership.

That might mean a broader service offering, a different geographic focus, a new customer segment, or a more consistent experience across locations.

It might also mean very little changes for customers immediately.

If the service, audience, and promise remain substantially the same, an urgent visual overhaul needs a clear reason.

If the business is changing direction, keeping every part of the old identity may create a different problem: the presentation continues to describe a company you are moving beyond.

Separate what has changed operationally from what needs to change visibly.

A change in ownership and a change in customer-facing identity are related decisions, but they are not interchangeable.

Find out what people already recognize

Before choosing a new direction, establish which parts of the existing brand have a useful role.

Speak with people who hear customer questions regularly, including the sales team, account managers, and customer service staff.

Ask existing customers how they describe the company and what helps them recognize it.

Review the website, proposals, vehicles, signage, uniforms, and other places where the identity appears.

  • Recognition: Which existing marks or visual details do customers recognize?
  • Visual identity: Is a symbol, color, or wordmark consistently associated with the business?
  • Reputation: What do customers expect to stay the same?
  • Confusion: What is unclear, outdated, or inconsistent today?
  • Direction: Does the current presentation fit the audience you want to serve next?

These questions give the design team something more useful than a general request to make the business look modern.

Decide how much of the identity to change

Start with the existing logo, typography, and colors, then judge what still supports the business.

Refine a recognizable logo

A familiar mark may need clearer proportions, simpler details, or more useful variations rather than a completely different idea.

Review the logo in a website header, proposal cover, small profile image, and important physical applications.

Keep the elements that help people recognize the business, and fix the parts that make the identity difficult to use.

Ask the designer to show the original and proposed versions in comparable applications so the decision is grounded in actual use.

Build a consistent typography and color system

A new logo alone will not resolve a website, presentation, and brochure that each look like a different company.

Define the typefaces, heading hierarchy, body-text treatment, and color roles that connect those materials.

Show how the palette works on light and dark backgrounds and which colors carry emphasis.

Test real headlines, longer service descriptions, and the smallest text your team needs to use.

Specify the supporting image direction too, so photography and graphics reinforce the same character.

Create a new direction when refinement is not enough

A more substantial redesign may be appropriate when the existing visual language no longer fits the audience, offer, or standard of the business.

Agree on those reasons before developing concepts, then evaluate the complete system rather than choosing an isolated symbol.

If several acquired businesses need to appear together, establish how their existing identities should coexist within shared layouts and materials.

A parent-brand endorsement may be one constraint, but the design task is to make that relationship clear through hierarchy, spacing, and consistent application.

Approve a visual direction that can support the website and everyday materials, not just a presentation slide.

Airport Executive: the logo before and after

Airport Executive shows how a business can change its presentation while retaining its existing name.

The London chauffeur service had more than 25 years of experience when we worked on its identity.

This example illustrates an identity redesign that retains the name; it does not establish an acquisition transaction.

We developed an aviation-inspired monogram, elegant typography, and a restrained visual system, together with website design.

The name stayed; the way the business presented itself changed.

You can see the broader system in the Airport Executive case study.

Connect the identity decision to the website

A new identity needs to work where customers learn about the business and decide what to do next.

Review the website’s service descriptions, company story, team information, and contact routes alongside the visual design.

Apply the approved typography, palette, image direction, and logo consistently across the website’s page types.

Keep familiar recognition cues where they help existing customers understand that they have reached the right business.

For any domain or URL changes, make migration planning an explicit responsibility in the website scope.

Do not let a logo approval stand in for approval of the entire customer experience.

Plan the transition in manageable stages

List the materials that need attention and give each one an owner, a dependency, and an intended release point.

Start with the places customers use to identify the company or make contact.

Then work through the sales materials, internal templates, physical applications, and less frequently used items.

A hypothetical rollout could begin with an agreed explanation of the change, continue with the website and core sales materials, and finish with a scheduled replacement of remaining applications.

The sequence should reflect how your business operates, rather than an arbitrary preference to unveil everything at once.

Where old and new materials will coexist, define what acceptable consistency looks like during the transition.

Give your team a short explanation they can use when customers ask what has changed.

Give your designer a decision-ready brief

A useful brief makes the important uncertainties visible before anyone starts drawing.

  • What is changing for the business and its customers?
  • Which logo, type, color, and image decisions are open for discussion?
  • What recognition or continuity should be preserved?
  • Where must the identity work alongside parent or sister brands?
  • Which website pages and physical applications need updating?
  • Who will approve the direction and consolidate feedback?
  • What must be ready first, and what can follow?

You do not need to solve every question before speaking with a designer.

You do need to distinguish fixed decisions from the decisions the project is meant to help you make.

A good rebrand should make the next version of the business clearer without discarding useful recognition by default.

If you are taking over an established business and need help connecting its identity and website to its next chapter, book a call to discuss which parts of the visual identity should stay, what needs redesigning, and how to approach the rollout.
